title: Try to appease rchk
description:
```
Package treesitter version 0.1.0
Package built using 87687/R 4.5.0; x86_64-pc-linux-gnu; 2025-02-06 00:23:21 UTC; unix   
Checked with rchk version 35618ebbccf3cd0b45a3530e6303970a22a9056b LLVM version 14.0.6
More information at https://github.com/kalibera/cran-checks/blob/master/rchk/PROTECT.md
For rchk in docker image see https://github.com/kalibera/rchk/blob/master/doc/DOCKER.md

Function ffi_query_matches
  [UP] unprotected variable elt while calling allocating function r_alloc_character.369 treesitter/src/query-matches.c:94
  [UP] unprotected variable elt while calling allocating function r_alloc_list.361 treesitter/src/query-matches.c:97
  [UP] unprotected variable names while calling allocating function r_alloc_list.361 treesitter/src/query-matches.c:97
  [UP] unprotected variable names while calling allocating function r_exec_new_node treesitter/src/query-matches.c:103
  [UP] unprotected variable nodes while calling allocating function r_exec_new_node treesitter/src/query-matches.c:103

Function r_exec_new_node
  [UP] allocating function r_env_find may destroy its unprotected argument (ns <arg 1>), which is later used. treesitter/src/node.c:395
  [UP] calling allocating function r_env_find with a fresh pointer (ns <arg 1>) treesitter/src/node.c:395
  [UP] unprotected variable ns while calling allocating function r_sym treesitter/src/node.c:395
  [UP] unprotected variable ns while calling allocating function Rf_lang3 treesitter/src/node.c:396
  [UP] unprotected variable ns while calling allocating function R_PreserveObject treesitter/src/node.c:397
  [UP] unprotected variable ns while calling allocating function _r_preserve treesitter/src/node.c:397
```

## r_env_find()

rchk thinks `r_env_find()` may allocate a fresh object (`ns`), I don't think it does in this particular case, but see https://github.com/kalibera/rchk/issues/36#issuecomment-2450203705

I think it's correct to just protect here

## r_dyn_list_push_back()

This one is a giant pain in the butt.

`r_dyn_list_push_back()` is a "real" function. It eventually calls `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` to store `elt`, but because `r_dyn_list_push_back()` is a real function there is some indirection between where `elt` is defined and where it is protected by `SET_VECTOR_ELT()`. This indirection causes rchk to think `elt` isn't actually protected, so when we try and use it later on (when we set `names` on it), rchk throws an error.

In rlang, `r_list_poke()` is defined as a macro for `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` to avoid this issue entirely. We thought maybe we could do that here as well by making `r_dyn_list_push_back()` and `r_dyn_list_poke()` macros as well, but it's complicated.

This was our first choice, but it doesn't work because `__elt` looks like a different object than `ELT` (which is `elt`) to rchk, so even though we call `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` on `__elt`, the original `elt` still looks unprotected to rchk.

```
#define r_dyn_list_push_back(P_VEC, ELT) do { \
  struct r_dyn_array* __p_vec = (P_VEC);      \
  r_obj* __elt = (ELT);                       \
  KEEP(__elt);                                \
  r_ssize __loc = r__dyn_increment(__p_vec);  \
  r_dyn_list_poke(__p_vec, __loc, __elt);     \
  FREE(1);                                    \
} while (0)
```

This was another option, but it's a huge footgun. We want to avoid double evaluation of `ELT`, which we do in the above version, but don't here. We commonly call this kind of function with something like `r_dyn_list_push_back(p_nodes, r_exec_new_node(capture.node, ffi_tree))`, which means `r_exec_new_node()` would be evaluated twice, so that rules this out.

```
#define r_dyn_list_push_back(P_VEC, ELT) do { \
  KEEP(ELT);                                  \
  r_ssize __loc = r__dyn_increment(P_VEC);    \
  r_dyn_list_poke(P_VEC, __loc, ELT);         \
  FREE(1);                                    \
} while (0)
```

Really I think this is a limitation of the rchk system. The best we can do is protect and document why we have to do so.

title: Replace `tree_edit()` with `parser_reparse()`
description:
Closes #8 

Because we treat trees as immutable, `tree_edit()` can really just get absorbed into `parser_parse()`. But then I realized that we could split `parser_parse()` into itself (without the `tree` argument) and `parser_reparse()` (with the required `tree` argument and the edit location) and that probably makes for a cleaner API overall.

Doing it this way removes the possibility for a `tree` to have invalid `text` that no longer aligns with its boundaries

title: Add ABI checks to `check_language()`
description:
Requires https://github.com/r-lib/tree-sitter-r/pull/124

With an automated system for updating the ABI version in `update-tree-sitter.R`

The idea is that a grammar package's language objects will now report their ABI version in an `abi` field. This is the ABI version when the `parser.c` was created. That allows us to then verify that ABI version against the version of the tree-sitter C library we ship _without having to try and load the pointer first_, which we are scared would otherwise have the potential to possibly crash R (even though memory alignment probably works in your favor here as long as new language fields are added to the end of the C level language object).

title: Try out batteries included approach
description:
With the goal of ensuring that the ABI of the tree-sitter bindings we ship will always be in sync with the ABI of the supported grammars' generated parser files.

Ideally we would ship {treesitter} separate from {treesitter.r} and friends, but R's package management system is not as locked down as other languages, and it is would be quite hard to ensure that users have compatible versions of both the bindings and whatever grammar package they are using. Worst case scenario is that they have an incompatible version that causes R to bomb immediately, with no indication of why.

This way ensures that whatever we send to CRAN will absolutely work, and updating the package updates all the grammars. We could also include a less safe method for hot loading your own grammar on the fly, which might be useful for testing tree-sitter-r itself, because we will want to be testing against the most recent dev version, not the version we end up bundling here. That would obviously allow languages that aren't officially supported to still work, provided the parser files are generated with a tree-sitter cli that has the same ABI as the bindings we ship in the package.

We should probably document the exact ABI version and tree-sitter commit that we ship. We could create a more official method of updating tree-sitter itself that could be in charge of that.

title: Test some queries aimed at identifying common testthat calls
description:
As discussed elsewhere, I'm adding tests for specific queries related to testthat usage. I've made a lot of choices, e.g. around helpers, that I'm happy to discuss and tweak. Having these queries under test is useful to me and I feel like it delivers some value for this package and the associated R grammar, more in the spirit of integration tests, I suppose.

The high level goal is to identify individual test atoms (meaning calls to `test_that()`, `describe()`, and `it()`, with their associated `desc` or `description`) and to get information on the tree, (meaning the parent `describe()` for each `it()` and whether a specific call is at the top-level or nested within another call). A very relevant testthat feature is the ability to run an individual `test_that()` or `describe()` via `testthat::test_file(desc =)`.

The query for `testthat::test_that()` is more ambitious, in terms of what it includes and excludes. The query for `describe(it())` is less so. This is partially because even a minimal `describe(it())` query has to be more complicated, by necessity. Also, I believe `test_that()` has vastly more usage, which makes it seem more worthwhile to contemplate a larger set of possibilities.

title: Bump minimum R version to 4.3.0
description:
tree-sitter requires C11 and is unlikely to change that https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter/pull/3339. C99 is old, so that's reasonable.

R's history with C99 is a big gnarly. R is currently at R 4.4.0 (released a month ago). Only as of R 4.3.0 (last year) did package authors gain a way to specify the C std version with `USE_Cxx` here:
https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/bacd56452465bd7fd95839c3e5dd1adf21be4de6/doc/NEWS.Rd#L1572-L1604

Additionally at that time, there was a change in R on Windows to allow the default C compiler to be used (typically C17 through RTools), rather than always defaulting to C99. For Mac and Linux, it was already doing this (and indeed for me it looks like a pretty new C std is being used):
https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/bacd56452465bd7fd95839c3e5dd1adf21be4de6/doc/NEWS.Rd#L1545-L1548

To try and guarantee Windows C11 support, we are raising the minimum R version to 4.3.0. 

I do not feel a need to specify a `USE_Cxx` field in `SystemRequirements`, as that specifies "use _up to_ this C standard" and we don't really want that - i.e. see the R NEWS linked above "Use a standard that is at most C17"
